title: Dividing property when a marriage ends
intro: This guide explains what Part I of Ontario's Family Law Act says about sharing the value of property when spouses separate, divorce or a spouse dies, and what the Family Law Rules require parties to disclose. It describes the law generally; it does not calculate anyone's entitlement.

sections.heading: Who Part I applies to
paragraphs: Part I (Family Property) uses the Act’s general definition of “spouse”: either of two persons who “are married to each other”, or who “have together entered into a marriage that is voidable or void, in good faith on the part of a person relying on this clause to assert any right.” (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))

Part I’s own definitions do not add unmarried partners. By contrast, the wider definition that includes two persons “who are not married to each other and have cohabited” is stated to apply “In this Part”, meaning Part III (Support Obligations). (Family Law Act, ss. 4 (1), 29)
For Part I, “court” means a court as defined in subsection 1 (1), “but does not include the Ontario Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))

sections.heading: Net family property and the valuation date
paragraphs: “Net family property” means “the value of all the property, except property described in subsection (2), that a spouse owns on the valuation date”, after deducting the spouse’s debts and other liabilities, and the value of property, “other than a matrimonial home”, that the spouse owned on the date of the marriage. That date-of-marriage value is net of the spouse’s debts and liabilities at that date, “other than debts or liabilities related directly to the acquisition or significant improvement of a matrimonial home”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
The liabilities deducted in calculating net family property “include any applicable contingent tax liabilities in respect of the property.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1.1))

The “valuation date” is “the earliest of” these dates: “The date the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation”; “The date a divorce is granted”; “The date the marriage is declared a nullity”; the date an application for improvident depletion is started that is later granted; and “The date before the date on which one of the spouses dies leaving the other spouse surviving.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))

“Property” is defined broadly as “any interest, present or future, vested or contingent, in real or personal property”. For a pension plan, it includes the “imputed value, for family law purposes, of the spouse’s interest in the plan”, for the period from the date of marriage to the valuation date. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
Values are calculated “as of close of business on that date.” If a spouse’s net family property comes to less than zero, “it shall be deemed to be equal to zero.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (4), (5))

sections.heading: Excluded property
paragraphs: Some property a spouse owns on the valuation date “does not form part of the spouse’s net family property”. The list includes property, “other than a matrimonial home, that was acquired by gift or inheritance from a third person after the date of the marriage”, and income from that property if the donor or testator “has expressly stated that it is to be excluded”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), paras. 1, 2)

The list also includes damages, or a right to damages, for personal injuries, nervous shock, mental distress or loss of guidance, care and companionship, or the part of a settlement that represents those damages. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), para. 3)

The list also includes certain life insurance proceeds payable on death; property, other than a matrimonial home, into which excluded property “can be traced”; “Property that the spouses have agreed by a domestic contract is not to be included in the spouse’s net family property”; and “Unadjusted pensionable earnings under the Canada Pension Plan.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), paras. 4-7)

The Act places the onus of proving a deduction from net family property, or an exclusion under subsection 4 (2), on the person claiming it: the onus “is on the person claiming it.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (3))

sections.heading: Equalization and unequal shares
paragraphs: When a divorce is granted, a marriage is declared a nullity, or the spouses are separated with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation, “the spouse whose net family property is the lesser of the two net family properties is entitled to one-half the difference between them.” The Act also provides for equalization when a spouse dies, and for serious danger of improvident depletion while spouses are cohabiting. (Family Law Act, s. 5 (1)-(3))

The Act states the purpose of section 5: to recognize that “child care, household management and financial provision are the joint responsibilities of the spouses” and that “inherent in the marital relationship there is equal contribution, whether financial or otherwise”, by the spouses to these responsibilities, “entitling each spouse to the equalization of the net family properties, subject only to the equitable considerations set out in subsection (6).” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (7))

The court “may award a spouse an amount that is more or less than half the difference between the net family properties if the court is of the opinion that equalizing the net family properties would be unconscionable”. The circumstances it has regard to include failure to disclose debts existing at marriage, debts “incurred recklessly or in bad faith”, gifts from the other spouse, and “a spouse’s intentional or reckless depletion of his or her net family property”. (Family Law Act, s. 5 (6) (a)-(d))

The other listed circumstances are an amount “disproportionately large in relation to a period of cohabitation that is less than five years”; one spouse incurring “a disproportionately larger amount of debts or other liabilities than the other spouse for the support of the family”; “a written agreement between the spouses that is not a domestic contract”; and “any other circumstance relating to the acquisition, disposition, preservation, maintenance or improvement of property.” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (6) (e)-(h))

sections.heading: Applying to the court and the time limits
paragraphs: “The court may, on the application of a spouse, former spouse or deceased spouse’s personal representative, determine any matter respecting the spouses’ entitlement under section 5.” (Family Law Act, s. 7 (1))

An application based on subsection 5 (1) or (2) “shall not be brought after the earliest of,” (a) “two years after the day the marriage is terminated by divorce or judgment of nullity”; (b) “six years after the day the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation”; (c) “six months after the first spouse’s death.” (Family Law Act, s. 7 (3))

Separately, the Act says the court “may, on motion, extend a time prescribed by this Act” if it is satisfied that “there are apparent grounds for relief”, that “relief is unavailable because of delay that has been incurred in good faith”, and that “no person will suffer substantial prejudice by reason of the delay.” (Family Law Act, s. 2 (8))

sections.heading: What the court can order
paragraphs: In an application under section 7, the court may order one spouse to pay the other the amount the court finds that spouse is entitled to, and that security be given. If “necessary to avoid hardship”, payment may be made in instalments or delayed for “a period not exceeding ten years”. If appropriate to satisfy an obligation imposed by the order, property may be transferred to a spouse, or “partitioned or sold”. (Family Law Act, s. 9 (1))

An order made under section 9 or 10 “shall not be made so as to require or result in the sale of an operating business or farm or so as to seriously impair its operation, unless there is no reasonable alternative method of satisfying the award.” (Family Law Act, s. 11 (1))

In an application under section 7 or 10, if the court “considers it necessary for the protection of the other spouse’s interests under this Part”, it may make an interim or final order “restraining the depletion of a spouse’s property” and for its “possession, delivering up, safekeeping and preservation”. (Family Law Act, s. 12)

Separately, a person may apply for a determination of a question with a spouse or former spouse “as to the ownership or right to possession of particular property, other than a question arising out of an equalization of net family properties under section 5”. (Family Law Act, s. 10 (1))

sections.heading: Financial disclosure
paragraphs: In an application under section 7, each party must serve and file a sworn or declared statement “disclosing particulars of” the party’s property, debts and other liabilities as of the date of marriage, the valuation date and the date of the statement; the deductions and exclusions claimed; and property disposed of “during the two years immediately preceding the making of the statement, or during the marriage, whichever period is shorter.” (Family Law Act, s. 8)

Under the Family Law Rules, when a document contains “a property claim”, the party making the claim “shall serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1)” with it, and the other party must do so within the time for responding. If there is a property claim, the financial statement “shall be in Form 13.1, whether a claim for support is also included or not.” (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (1), (1.2))

For a Part I claim, unless the court orders otherwise, a party must, “no later than 30 days after the day by which the financial statement is required to be served”, serve further documents. These include statements closest to the valuation date for accounts, savings and investments; pension valuation requests; property assessments; business, partnership, corporation and trust records; “Documentation that supports a claim, if any, for an exclusion under subsection 4 (2) of the Family Law Act”; debt statements; and proof of date-of-marriage values. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (3.3))

A party serving these documents confirms service with “a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A)”. If a party thinks the other’s disclosure is not enough, “the party shall make a request in writing to the other party for the necessary additional information”, and if it is not given “within seven days of the request”, the court may order it. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (5.0.2), (11))

sections.heading: Agreements about property
paragraphs: Marriage contracts, cohabitation agreements and separation agreements may each deal with “ownership in or division of property”. A domestic contract is “unenforceable unless made in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed.” (Family Law Act, ss. 52 (1) (a), 53 (1) (a), 54 (a), 55 (1))

“A domestic contract dealing with a matter that is also dealt with in this Act prevails unless this Act provides otherwise.” Property the spouses have agreed by domestic contract is not to be included is excluded property. (Family Law Act, ss. 2 (10), 4 (2), para. 6)

A court may, on application, set aside a domestic contract or a provision in it “if a party failed to disclose to the other significant assets, or significant debts or other liabilities, existing when the domestic contract was made”, “if a party did not understand the nature or consequences of the domestic contract”, or “otherwise in accordance with the law of contract.” (Family Law Act, s. 56 (4))
